topic: Corporate, Securities, and Commercial Law: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
description: This module introduces the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. It covers the essential characteristics of Promissory Notes, Bills of Exchange, and Cheques. It also emphasizes the highly privileged position of a 'Holder in Due Course' and the stringent criminal provisions and timelines regarding the dishonour of cheques under Section 138.

key_points: Promissory Note (Section 4): An instrument in writing containing an unconditional 'undertaking' (promise), signed by the maker, to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person, or to the bearer of the instrument.

Bill of Exchange (Section 5): An instrument in writing containing an unconditional 'order', signed by the maker, directing a certain person to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person or to the bearer.
Cheque (Section 6): A cheque is essentially a bill of exchange that is drawn on a specified banker and is always payable on demand.

holder_in_due_course.concept: Holder vs. Holder in Due Course (HDC)
key_points: Holder (Section 8): Any person who is legally entitled in their own name to the possession of the instrument and to receive or recover the amount due on it.

Holder in Due Course (Section 9): A person who acquires a negotiable instrument for valuable 'consideration' (value), 'before maturity', and in 'good faith' (without sufficient cause to believe that any defect existed in the title of the person transferring it).

Privilege of HDC: The most important rule of the NI Act is that a Holder in Due Course gets a 'clean title'. They acquire the instrument free from all prior defects in title (e.g., even if the instrument was previously obtained by fraud by an earlier party, the HDC can still legally recover the money).

Criminal Offence: Bouncing of a cheque due to insufficient funds (or if it exceeds the arranged limit) is a criminal offence. The punishment is imprisonment for a term up to 2 years, or a fine up to twice the amount of the cheque, or both.
Statutory Timelines (Crucial): To file a case under Sec 138, strict timelines must be followed.
Step 1: The cheque must be presented to the bank within its validity period (3 months).
Step 2: The payee must send a legal demand notice to the drawer within 30 days of receiving the return memo from the bank.

Step 3: The drawer is given 15 days from the receipt of the notice to make the payment. If they fail, the cause of action arises, and the payee has exactly 30 days to file a criminal complaint in court.

questions.question: What is the primary difference in the core wording between a Promissory Note and a Bill of Exchange under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881?

options.A: A Promissory Note contains an unconditional 'order' to pay, while a Bill of Exchange contains an unconditional 'undertaking' to pay.
options.B: A Promissory Note contains an unconditional 'undertaking' (promise) to pay, while a Bill of Exchange contains an unconditional 'order' to pay.
options.C: A Promissory Note is oral, whereas a Bill of Exchange must be in writing.
options.D: A Promissory Note involves three parties, while a Bill of Exchange involves only two.

questions.explanation: According to Sections 4 and 5 of the NI Act, a Promissory Note is a promise (undertaking) made by the debtor to pay the creditor. A Bill of Exchange is an order made by the creditor directing the debtor to pay.

questions.question: Ravi finds a bearer cheque dropped by someone on the street. He uses this cheque to buy a new laptop from an electronics store. The store owner accepts the cheque in good faith, providing the laptop to Ravi without knowing the cheque was lost/found. Can the store owner legally recover the money?

options.A: No, because the store owner received a cheque that originally had a defective title (found/stolen).
options.B: No, the true owner of the cheque can easily claim the money back from the store owner.
options.C: Yes, because the store owner took the cheque for value, before maturity, and in good faith, making them a 'Holder in Due Course' with a clean title.
options.D: Yes, but the store owner must split the amount with the true owner of the cheque.

questions.explanation: This demonstrates the core privilege of a Holder in Due Course (HDC). Even though Ravi's title to the cheque was defective, because the store owner acquired it for consideration (the laptop), in good faith, and without notice of the defect, the store owner gets a perfect title and can recover the money.

questions.question: Priya deposits a cheque given to her by a client. On March 1st, she receives a memo from her bank stating the cheque has bounced due to 'insufficient funds'. What is the mandatory next step Priya must take, and within what timeframe, to maintain her right to file a criminal case under Section 138 of the NI Act?

options.A: She must immediately file an FIR at the local police station within 15 days.
options.B: She must send a statutory legal demand notice to the drawer (client) demanding the money within 30 days of receiving the bank memo.
options.C: She must file a case directly in the Magistrate court within 90 days of the cheque bouncing.
options.D: She must wait for the client to issue a new cheque within 45 days.

questions.explanation: Under Section 138 of the NI Act, a criminal complaint cannot be filed directly or immediately. The payee MUST issue a statutory legal notice in writing to the drawer demanding the cheque amount within 30 days of receiving information from the bank about the dishonour. Only if the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of receiving this notice can a case be filed.
